nodes.title: Node distribution: the backend behind the Node Builder
nodes.body:
Draft PR: rocketride-org/rocketride-server#2245 ## What this backend is It makes a node that **one person uploaded** show up and work on **someone else's machine**. That is the whole job. Four pieces: | # | Piece | Surface | State | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | **Store it** — take the zip, version it, keep it | `rrext_deploy` | built | | 2 | **Decide who can use it** — mine, my team's, public | `rrext_deploy_node` | built | | 3 | **Fetch and run it** when a pipeline names a node the machine does not have | the resolver | designed | | 4 | **Show it in the picker** so the designer has something to draw | `rrext_services` | half | Piece 3 is the one that needs a decision from the engine side — a single binding, described below. **The package is the node directory itself** — zipped as it sits, with `services.json` at the root. No wrapper, no imposed layout: what the author has on disk is what travels, and it comes back out the same shape. **A run keeps nothing.** It materialises only the nodes it names, and drops them afterwards. > **Two separate places, easy to conflate.** > > **The server** is where a node is stored, versioned, and where reach is decided — yours, your team's, or public. That is the whole of distribution and permissions. > > **A working folder on whichever machine runs the pipeline** is where a copy gets unzipped so Python can import it, and it is deleted when the run ends. It holds no permissions and distributes nothing. --- ## One node, end to end A node called `ticket_feed`, from the folder on disk to the run that uses it. Every name and path below is literal. ### 1 · It is created here One directory, carrying its manifest and its own requirements: ``` /nodes/ticket_feed/ services.json protocol "ticket_feed://" IGlobal.py IInstance.py requirements.txt ``` Nothing about this step is new — this is a developer's own workspace, before anything is published. ### 2 · It is packaged and published — one call ```js await client.deploy.addNode('nodes/ticket_feed', { deployTo: 'Platform' }) // ↓ packs the folder, then rrext_deploy · "add" · kind "node" ``` Packing lives in `rocketride/app-pack` beside the app packer, so a UI, the CLI and CI produce byte-identical bundles. **The node folder is the zip root** — not its parent — which puts `services.json` at the top, where the server reads identity from. `.gitignore` is honoured and Python's own leavings (`__pycache__`, `.pyc`) never ship. The id comes from `protocol` in the zip's own manifest. The request cannot name a different one, whatever it says. ### 3 · It lands here on the server ``` orgs//files/.deployments/ticket_feed/ v000003-a1b2c3d4.json the artifact — id, name, version, runtime, requirements, sha256 v000003-a1b2c3d4/bundle/ticket_feed-v000003.zip retained transport v000003-a1b2c3d4/source/services.json, IInstance.py, … unpacked ``` Same registry apps and pipes use. The version is immutable, and inert until something is pinned to it — which the `deployTo` in step 2 did. **This is the node's real home, and where reach is decided.** Pinned to you, to a team, or to public, one node can hold all three at once. Everything after this step is machines fetching a copy. ### 4 · It becomes available ```js resolve_node_pins(orgId, userId, teamIds) // → [{ id: "ticket_feed", version: 3, nodeVersion: "1.2.0", // runtime: "python", requirements: ["httpx"], rung: "team", … }] ``` This is the picker's feed. One entry per node, best version already chosen. ### 5 · A run uses it A pipeline names `ticket_feed` on a machine that does not have it. The resolver fetches, verifies the sha256, unpacks, and writes: ``` /nodes/ticket_feed/ the directory from step 1, restored ``` Identical to step 1, which is why the manifest's `path` never has to be rewritten. When the run ends, the run root goes. --- ## What there is to build against Every call below is built and tested. The right column is what it is *for* — if a surface is missing from this list, it does not exist yet. | Call | Returns | Feeds | |---|---|---| | `resolve_node_pins` | Every node this caller can use, one entry per node, best version already chosen | The palette / picker | | `deploy_node · versions` | The version rail, newest first, with who published and when | Version list on the node's card | | `deploy_node · where` | Which audience holds which version | "Deployed to" panel | | `deploy.addNode(folder)` | Packs the folder and deploys it, optionally bound in the same call | The Deploy button | | `deploy.add({kind:'node', data})` | The same, when you already hold the bytes | CI, scripts | | `deploy_node · deploy` | The binding that now serves | Deploy to team… / rollback | | `deploy_node · disable` / `remove` | The withdrawn binding | Unpublish | One entry from the picker feed: ```json { "id": "ticket_feed", "name": "Ticket Feed", "version": 3, "nodeVersion": "1.2.0", "runtime": "python", "requirements": ["httpx"], "bundleSha256": "…", "orgId": "acme", "rung": "team" } ``` `rung` is there so the UI can say *why* a node is available — your own, your team's, or public — which is also what tells someone whether they may withdraw it. --- ## Both halves Publishing is deliberate and done by a person. Resolving is automatic and happens per run. They only meet at the registry. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant B as Node Builder participant S as Server participant R as Registry participant E as Engine Note over B,R: Publish — deliberate B->>S: rrext_deploy add (kind=node, zip) S->>S: guard zip, read services.json S->>R: immutable version + bundle B->>S: rrext_deploy_node deploy (pin an audience) Note over E,R: Run — automatic, only what this pipeline names E->>E: providers the engine does not know E->>R: which version is pinned for this caller? R-->>E: version + sha256 E->>S: fetch bundle E->>E: verify sha256, guard, unpack E->>E: place in the run folder, rescan E->>E: run, then drop the run tree ``` --- ## Resolution at pipeline start Order matters: verify (5) precedes unpack (6). | # | Step | Detail | |---|---|---| | 1 | Detect | Each component's `provider` minus what the engine knows. Nothing missing → immediate return. | | 2 | Look up | The version that caller's pins resolve to. No pin → run stops, naming the node and the org searched. | | 3 | Reuse | Cache keyed `/`. Immutable by construction, never invalidated. | | 4 | Fetch | The stored bundle — filesystem on OSS, S3/Azure on cloud. No second storage path. | | 5 | Verify | sha256 against the artifact digest. Mismatch refuses before anything is unpacked. | | 6 | Guard | Same archive checks publish applies. Publish was a different moment; this one gets its own. | | 7 | Materialise | The directory is written into the run's own folder, in the layout the engine already imports from. | | 8 | Rescan | The one engine-side piece. Everything above and below it is written. | | 9 | Clean | Run root dropped with the run; cache persists. | Steps 1–7 and 9 are Python. Step 8 is the only engine change. --- ## What resolution needs from the engine **Nothing here is about storage or permissions** — those are settled on the server before a run ever starts. This is only the folder Python imports from, on whichever machine is executing. | Needed | Why | |---|---| | The run's tree reachable as a node path | `--node_path` is a single option read at process start. If the engine was started without one, or with a different one, a run tree elsewhere is invisible. This is the argument for the rescan binding taking a directory. | | Rescan after writing | Service definitions are built at startup. Without a rescan the files are on disk and the engine does not know. | | Reach child processes | `task_engine` hands `--node_path` down to children; a node resolved for the parent has to arrive the same way. | Two of those three are Python. Only the rescan is engine-side. --- ## The rescan binding The bindings expose `getServiceDefinitions()`, which reads schemas that are *already built*. A node can be put on disk from Python, and the engine cannot be told to notice it. Reading a node off disk happens in `loadServices()`, a lambda inside `IServices::init()` — the same one that walks the node tree at startup. (`updateDefinitions()` is not the one: it rebuilds JSON schemas from what is already in memory and never touches the disk.) **The change is a method that scans a directory it is handed, then runs the schema rebuild that already follows it.** No new logic — `init()` performs both steps today. Taking a directory rather than re-reading the option is also what makes it work on a cloud worker, and the same call is what "appears in the palette without a restart" needs — so one binding serves every path a node can arrive by. > `--node_path` is a single option fixed at process start. If the binding re-reads that option, the run tree must live under whatever path the engine was started with — and fails outright if it was started with none. **Recommendation: have it take a directory argument**, same size of change, independent of how the engine was launched. --- ## OSS and SaaS This has to work self-hosted as well as it works on cloud, so it is worth saying exactly how that is guaranteed rather than hoped for. **There is one code path, not two.** Every registry and binding call this uses — nine of them — is declared on `AccountBase` and implemented by both `account/oss/` and `extension/saas/`. The node code never asks which one it is talking to, the same way the app rail never does. Storage is the same story: one Store, filesystem when self-hosted, S3 or Azure on cloud. **OSS is not a degraded case.** It supplies a real identity — user `local`, org `local`, a `local` team, and a developer id. So `@me` and `@team/local` resolve normally, and `@public` is held to the same namespace rule it is held to on cloud rather than being waved through. Nothing about reach behaves differently; there is simply one team to reach. | Where they genuinely differ | Consequence | |---|---| | **The content cache** | Self-hosted, it lives on the developer's machine and survives. On cloud, workers are ephemeral: the cache dies with the pod and every run re-downloads. Either accept that (bundles are small and the store is close) or give workers a shared volume. Worth deciding, not discovering. | | **Whether a workspace exists** | A developer's engine is usually started with `--node_path` pointing at their workspace. **A cloud worker has no workspace and no such option.** If the rescan binding re-reads that option, resolution cannot work on cloud at all. This is the strongest argument for it taking a directory instead. | --- ## Zip validation Strict validation before anything is decompressed. What is enforced today, on publish and again on fetch: | Check | State | |---|---| | No `..` segments, no absolute paths | built | | File-count ceiling | built | | Real decompressed bytes, not the sizes the archive claims | built | | sha256 recorded at publish, checked before unpacking | built | These are facts about the archive. Anything beyond them is a judgement about *content* — whether a node may run code at install time, or shell out, or pull a dependency that has to compile. Worth deciding whether that belongs in this work at all. --- ## Reach, and how availability resolves A node can hold several bindings at once. The picker feed resolves them the way apps do: walk `@public`, then each of the caller's teams, then the caller, and the **more specific rung wins** a node-id collision — user beats team beats public. A same-rung tie breaks on the lowest org id, so a stray public row cannot displace a lower org's claim on a name. A binding serves only when it is enabled **and** its version is serveable: public reach demands a `ready` version, internal reach accepts anything that did not fail. That gate matters more later than now — a Python node is born ready; a compiled one will not be. | Target | Requirement to publish or withdraw there | |---|---| | `@me` | Authenticated session | | `@team/` | Membership of that team | | `@public` | Registered developer org owning the node's namespace | | `@org` | Does not exist — use an org-admin-maintained team | Private reach needs no namespace: the registry is partitioned by org. Public reach is one shared space, so a node there must sit in the developer namespace. Looser than apps by design — app ids are always namespaced, node ids are their protocol. --- ## Unpublishing and changing reach Reach is not a level that moves up and down. It is a **set of independent bindings**: a node can sit on `@me`, `@team/Platform` and `@public` at the same time, each pointing at its own version. | Intent | Call | |---|---| | Widen reach | `deploy` with the broader target — adds a binding, leaves the others | | Narrow reach | `disable` or `remove` on the target being dropped | | Change version for one audience | `deploy` again with a different version — this is also rollback | | Stop serving, keep it recoverable | `disable` — reversible, bind again and it is back | | Take it out of the listing | `remove` | | See every binding | `where` | **Withdrawal never touches the version.** Published versions are immutable and stay on the registry, which is what keeps rollback possible: pulling a node from a team today does not stop you pinning that same version tomorrow. Withdrawal is gated exactly like publishing — dropping a `@public` binding needs the same standing that granting it did. --- ## The open problems, and how each resolves Every gap this design had, with the answer I would build. Three of the seven need agreement because they touch the UI side or change behaviour; the rest are mine to close. | Problem | Resolution | Needs a decision | |---|---|---| | **Storage credentials**
A run has no logged-in session to borrow credentials from. | No new credential path is needed. `TASK_CONTROL` already carries `userId`, `teamId` and `orgId` into every run, including scheduled ones, and the bundle is read through the same Store the server uses, scoped to that org. What is missing is plumbing the run's org into the resolver — wiring, not a mechanism. | — | | **`.RRnode`**
The file that opens the node canvas. | A small JSON at the root of the node directory, mirroring `.rrapp`: it points at the directory and opens the canvas. **The backend ignores it entirely** — `services.json` stays the single source of identity. Two files each claiming to say what a node is called is the failure worth designing out now. | yes | | **Concurrent runs**
Two runs resolving the same node at once. | The cache is keyed by digest, with one lock per key — the same `FileLock` the dependency installer already uses, so the cross-platform behaviour is proven. Unpack into a temp directory and rename into place; the second run waits and then reuses. | — | | **Child processes**
A node resolved for the parent has to reach the children. | The run's folder becomes the process's node path, which `task_engine` already hands down to children. If the engine was started with one already, materialise inside it rather than creating a second — one path is all the option allows. | — | | **Cache lifetime**
Nothing removes what is downloaded, and on cloud nothing keeps it either. | A size ceiling with least-recently-used eviction, swept after a run rather than during one. Safe precisely because entries are content-addressed: deleting one can only ever cost a re-download, never correctness. On cloud the pod is ephemeral and the cache is effectively a per-run optimisation — fine, but a deliberate answer rather than the same answer. | yes | | **Who uses this node**
Withdrawing breaks pipelines with no warning. | Not by scanning pipelines — a static answer goes stale the moment someone edits one. **Record what each run actually resolved.** Then the question reports real usage, it costs nothing extra because the resolver already knows, and the panel on the node card has something true to show. | yes | | **Withdraw everywhere**
Unpublishing is one call per audience. | `target: "@all"` on `disable` and `remove`: read the current pins, check permission on *every* one before touching any, then withdraw them. It fails whole rather than half — a node left public because the loop stopped midway is the worst outcome available. | — | --- ## The modules | Module | What it holds | |---|---| | `account/node_deploy.py` | The `kind:'node'` adapter: publishing, the control verbs, and `resolve_node_pins` | | `account/node_resolve.py` | Resolution for a run — deciding, then fetching and placing | | `account/deploy_common.py` | The one seam for what both deploy rails share | | `modules/task/commands/cmd_node.py` | Thin DAP router for `rrext_deploy_node` | | `cli/commands/node.ts` | The `rocketride node` group | | `client/deploy.ts` | `addNode` plus the four control methods on the SDK's deploy namespace | | `app-pack/index.ts` | `packNodeSource` — the packing rules, beside the app packer | | `client-python/mixins/nodes.py` | The same control surface for the Python SDK | Two of these are worth a word on why they exist as separate things. **`node_resolve` is split from `node_deploy`** because publishing and resolving meet only at the registry. Deciding what a run needs is pure — a pipeline dict, the names the engine carries, the caller's pins — so it can answer "will this run work?" without reaching the network or the disk, and the fetching half gets one clear input. **`deploy_common` exists** because node publishing needs the same identity, audience and archive checks app publishing does. Those answers live in `app_deploy`, which got them first. One import to find beats six scattered call sites, and the public names are the ones they will keep if the implementations are ever lifted across. --- ## How to try it ### The tests 87 of them, against the engine's own interpreter — not the system Python, which does not have the `ai` package: ``` ./dist/server/engine -m pytest packages/ai/tests/ai/account/test_node_deploy.py packages/ai/tests/ai/account/test_node_resolve.py -q ``` ### Publishing Point it at the folder — packing is the SDK's job, so nothing has to zip anything by hand: ``` rocketride node add nodes/ticket_feed --comment "first cut" rocketride node add nodes/ticket_feed --deploy-to ``` The second form publishes and binds in one call; without it the version publishes **inert** and the command says so rather than letting anyone assume it is live. The id comes from the zip's own manifest, so publishing under someone else's node name is not possible regardless of what the request says. `deploy add --kind node` still takes a zip you already hold, for CI. Things worth checking while you are there: publishing the same node twice gives you v1 and v2 rather than overwriting; a zip with no `services.json` at its root is refused and leaves nothing behind; and a zip carrying an `overrides.txt` is refused outright. ### Controlling it afterwards ``` rocketride node add nodes/ticket_feed --deploy-to rocketride node versions ticket_feed rocketride node deploy ticket_feed 3 --target @team/Platform rocketride node where ticket_feed rocketride node disable ticket_feed --target @team/Platform rocketride node remove ticket_feed --target @all ``` `--target @all` withdraws every binding the node has, checking permission on all of them before touching any — it withdraws all or none. Worth trying: pin v1 after v2 and watch rollback be the same verb; `disable` then `deploy` again and watch it come back; and confirm that after any withdrawal `node versions` still lists everything, because withdrawal acts on the binding and never on the version. The same surface is on the SDK as `client.deploy.nodeVersions` / `nodeDeploy` / `nodeWhere` / `nodeWithdraw`, which is what a UI would call. ### What cannot be tried yet **The full round trip.** A pipeline naming a published node will fetch it, verify it, install its dependencies and place it correctly — and then the engine will not know it is there, because the rescan has nowhere to call. --- ## Status | | | |---|---| | done | Publish a version — manifest identity, content beside the artifact, compensation on failure | | done | See, pin, locate, withdraw | | done | `deployTo` on publish | | done | Which nodes a caller has — one scope walk, shared by picker and resolver | | done | Node dependencies recorded on the artifact; `overrides.txt` refused | | done | Resolution at pipeline start — detect, look up, fetch, verify, guard, cache, install deps, place, clean | | done | Withdraw from every audience in one call | | blocked | The rescan — needs the engine-side method above | | open | Published nodes in the picker — the feed exists; injecting it into what `rrext_services` serves does not | | open | App-scoped vs general nodes | ## Tests **140 tests** — 89 on the engine, 26 on connection wiring, 17 in the TypeScript SDK, 8 in the Python SDK. The engine ones run against its own interpreter. Fakes follow `test_app_deploy.py`: an in-memory registry over the account singleton, and the **real** Store over a temp filesystem — so a call against a method the store does not have fails in the test the way it would live. | Area | n | What is pinned | |---|---|---| | Artifact | 5 | Identity comes from the manifest, not the caller; runtime and digest recorded | | Content | 3 | Transport zip retained, source unpacked, both beside their artifact | | Refusals | 8 | Unauthenticated, missing/text data, non-zip, no manifest, traversal, unsafe id — each leaving nothing behind | | Requirements | 5 | Declared deps on the artifact; `overrides.txt` refused; size cap | | deployTo | 6 | Bare team resolves, binds the version just published, failed bind leaves it published | | Versions / where | 4 | Rail newest-first, node's own version, empty rail, pin listing | | Deploy | 5 | Default target, unknown version, rollback is the same verb | | Withdrawal | 4 | disable / remove act on the binding, never the version | | Reach | 6 | Public needs the namespace; withdrawal gated identically | | Availability | 10 | Scope walk precedence, disabled and failed never serve, public needs ready | The resolver's own tests publish a node through the real publish path and resolve it back over the **real** Store, rather than a fake on both sides: publish and resolve agree on where a bundle lives only by convention, and that convention needs something watching it. The client tests cover both halves of what can drift there: packing runs against a **real temp directory**, because the two rules that matter — the node folder is the zip root, and Python's leavings never ship — are only observable on disk; the control calls run against a recording stub, since the server's behaviour is pinned by the engine suite and what can drift is the argument names. ``` npx jest tests/node-distribution.test.ts # TypeScript ./dist/server/engine -m pytest packages/client-python/tests/test_nodes_mixin.py -q ``` What is **not** covered, because it is not written: the rescan. --- ## What review turned up CodeRabbit found one bug that mattered a great deal, and it is worth recording because of *why* it survived. `TaskConn` initialises its command mixins by hand. `NodeCommands` had no constructor of its own, so that call fell through to `DAPConn.__init__`, which takes one positional argument and was handed three. **Every connection would have died with a TypeError** — not node publishing, the whole engine. Nothing caught it because the command tests all use connection stand-ins; nothing builds the real class. So the fix landed with the invariant rather than alone: a mixin `TaskConn` initialises explicitly must own a three-argument constructor. That covers all twelve today and whatever is added next, and it was verified by putting the bug back and watching it fail. Three more, all real: | Found | Why it mattered | |---|---| | An **empty digest** borrowed a warm cache | It joined to the node's *own* directory, which holds the digest slots — copied out, a folder of hashes pretending to be a node, and it happened before the digest was checked. Digests are now validated as the path segments they are, which also closes anything climbing out of the cache root. | | Dependency installs were **unbounded** | A stalled resolver hung the run with nothing to show for it. Now bounded — though the installer process itself survives, because `depends` drives uv through subprocess calls that take no timeout. That deadline belongs there. | | The packer could **ship without a manifest** | `services.json` was checked against the filesystem, not against what the pack selects. An ignore rule could swallow it, and the server would refuse the bundle for a reason nobody would trace back to a `.gitignore` line. | Two findings were declined with reasons rather than fixed: gating publishing on `task.control` (the app rail checks exactly the same thing — diverging on nodes alone would be worse than the consistency we have, and a published version is inert until pinned), and one artifact read per version in the rail (trivial, and the app rail reads the same way). --- ## Closing the last gap The rescan lands **on this same branch**, not beside it. A backend that cannot tell the engine to look is not a backend that works, and splitting it would leave two pieces someone has to remember to merge in the right order. The care goes into how the change is shaped instead: 1. **A new method, `init()` untouched.** It repeats the few lines that scan a node directory rather than reorganising the ones that exist. Less tidy, and the engine's startup path stays byte for byte as it is — unifying them later is cheap, and breaking startup is not. 2. **It lands with no callers.** The binding goes in first, invoked by nothing. A change nobody calls cannot break anybody. 3. **Checked A/B**: the same services discovered before and after, plus a real pipeline run — compiling is not evidence. 4. **Then one further commit** wires resolution to it. If any of this has to come out, it is two clean reverts and the rest of the branch stands. ## Decisions this needs 1. **Rescan binding** — directory argument vs re-reading `--node_path`. Recommendation above. 2. **Where a run materialises a node**, and whether anything is kept between runs. 3. **`.RRnode` carries no identity** — it opens the canvas; `services.json` stays the only thing that says what a node is called. 4. **Usage is recorded, not scanned** — "which pipelines use this node" answered from what runs actually resolved, rather than from reading pipelines. 5. **Pipeline names a node with no pin** — current assumption: the run fails, naming the node and the org searched. The alternative is that the resolver looks beyond the caller's own org, which changes the permission model. 6. **Validation depth** — whether checks on node *content* (install-time hooks, dynamic import, wheels-only deps) belong in this work or a later one. --- *Branch `feat/node-deploy` · 19 commits · 140 tests · draft PR #2245.*

nodes.title: Guild → Teams revamp: multi-tenant self-serve product, Battle.net auth, React rewrite
nodes.body:
Consolidating a planning conversation into one place since it touches, and probably supersedes/merges, #450 (build step) and #570 (productization).

## Core structure: Guild → Teams

Move away from a single-guild site to a real multi-tenant hierarchy:

```
Guild (tenant)              one Blizzard guild/realm, one Battle.net roster sync, optional Discord server
 ├─ Team (Phoenix)          own roster, loot config, calendar
 ├─ Team (Immolation)       separate roster/loot/calendar, same guild
 └─ Team (...)              officers can add more without a new signup
```

This is a deliberate difference from Viserio, which is one-group-per-team with no guild layer above it — WGA already runs two teams under one guild informally, so this formalizes real usage instead of Viserio's flatter model.

## Auth: Battle.net over Discord

Primary sign-in switches to Battle.net OAuth. It gives verified character ownership straight from Blizzard, which removes the manual "claim your character + officer review" step entirely. Discord stays as an optional connected integration (bot notifications/raid-night pings), not identity.

## Permissions: fully manual grants, no rank-derivation

Considered auto-granting site permissions from in-game Blizzard guild rank, and walked it back — officer status belongs to the person, not a rank snapshot, and giving a raider-officer broad guild privileges by default isn't the right default. Landed on:
- **Guild-level roles**: Owner, Admin, Member — granted explicitly by the Guild Owner/Admin.
- **Team-level roles**: Officer, Raider, Viewer — granted explicitly, scoped to one team.
- Blizzard in-game rank shows as informational metadata only, grants nothing.
- Roles attach to a Battle.net account (a person), not a character, so there's no "which character's rank counts" ambiguity.

## Onboarding flow

1. Sign in with Battle.net → create guild → Blizzard roster sync (region + realm + guild name → full character roster).
2. Guild Owner invites specific people and assigns roles.
3. Team Officers configure their own team (raid nights, loot rules, roster assignment from the guild's synced character pool).

## New features this unlocks

- **Blizzard guild-level roster sync** — one sync serves every team under the guild; teams assign a subset as their raid roster. Also pulls live gear/enchant/ilvl via the Character Equipment API, powering a "needs attention: N missing enchants, N empty sockets" audit similar to Viserio's.
- **Sim import** — paste a Raidbots Droptimizer report, auto-parsed per-item upgrade %, replacing the current manual raidbots/wowhead-link-plus-officer-review BiS flow (manual link stays as a fallback).
- Cross-team guild admin access, closing #607 properly instead of special-casing it.
- Candidates pulled from comparing current WGA features against Viserio: multi-night "time away" vacation tracking, M+ key/vault tracking (current M+ tab is exclusions-only), an officer task board ("what we need from you" on the raider's personal dashboard), a personal "You" landing view instead of team-wide.

## Route map (draft)

```
/                                    marketing/login
/join/:code                          invite redemption
/guilds                              "my guilds" dashboard
/guilds/new
/guilds/:guildId                     Guild Hub
/guilds/:guildId/teams/new
/guilds/:guildId/settings/{general,members,integrations}
/guilds/:guildId/teams/:teamId               team home
/guilds/:guildId/teams/:teamId/{roster,signup,streams,history,about,news,help}
/guilds/:guildId/teams/:teamId/manage/...    officer pages, scoped to this team
/guilds/:guildId/teams/:teamId/settings/...  raid nights, claim mode, loot targets
/account
```

## Billing — leaning toward pooled/metered-by-guild (inspired by WowUtils)

Individual supporter tiers grant personal perks + contribute "boost points" to a shared **guild-level** pool; the pool's tier unlocks group-wide capacity/speed (Blizzard sync frequency, sim-import queue priority, auto WCL sync, roster size caps, loot history retention) rather than gating features outright. Free tier stays fully functional, just slower/smaller/manual-refresh. One generous supporter can carry the whole guild's tier, which fits how guilds already behave (one or two people usually carry paid tool costs today). Not decided: actual price points, quota numbers, whether pooling is guild-level or per-team.

## Still open

- Multi-tenancy schema: Option A (clone per customer) vs. B (shared DB, guild_id-scoped) — this whole plan only works as B.
- Hosting off GitHub Pages — needed regardless for per-guild/team routing + real cache-control headers.
- Battle.net OAuth region-locking assumptions.
- React rewrite (#450) is the underlying enabler for all of this — routing, multi-tenant state, and this scale of nav restructuring don't work well on the current globals+innerHTML architecture.

Open to feedback on any piece of this — structure, permissions, billing shape, or things I've missed from what Viserio/WowUtils already do well.

nodes.title: Wheels 4.0 — multi-tenancy as a framework feature
nodes.body:
Multi-tenancy in 4.0 is in the framework, not in a plugin or community package. This post walks through the seam framing, how per-request datasource switching composes with the rest of the framework, the three deployment models supported, the deliberate escape hatches, and how 4.0 differs from the Rails / Laravel / Django approaches.

## Multi-tenancy is a seam problem

You need exactly one seam that catches every query, every job, every background task. Miss one — the straggler query in a report action, the `CreateObject("java", ...)` that goes around the ORM, the background job enqueued from a request that never asked whose tenant it was — and customer A sees customer B's invoice on a Sunday afternoon.

Plugin-based tenancy catches about eighty percent of the data paths. The hard twenty percent only gets caught when the seam lives below the consumer code, in the framework itself.

## How resolution works

[#1951](https://github.com/wheels-dev/wheels/pull/1951) — per-request datasource switching at the framework core. A tenant resolver runs in middleware before the controller instantiates. The resolved tenant attaches to the request, and the datasource resolver picks it up.

```cfm
// config/settings.cfm
set(middleware = [new app.middleware.TenantResolver()]);

// app/middleware/TenantResolver.cfc
component implements="wheels.middleware.MiddlewareInterface" {
    public any function handle(required struct request, required any next) {
        var subdomain = ListFirst(arguments.request.cgi.server_name, ".");
        arguments.request.tenant = subdomain;
        $setTenantDatasource(arguments.request.tenant);
        return arguments.next(arguments.request);
    }
}
```

The resolution source is up to you: subdomain (`acme.myapp.com`), path prefix (`/t/acme`), request header (`X-Tenant: acme`), or a claim out of a JWT (`tid`). Same middleware contract — pull the identifier, call `$setTenantDatasource`, pass the request along.

## Three SaaS data patterns supported

You pick by isolation requirement, not by framework limit.

- **Separate database per tenant** — cleanest isolation. Per-customer backup and restore, per-customer performance tuning, per-customer encryption at rest. The datasource resolver switches the entire connection per request. GDPR erasure is a `DROP DATABASE` away from complete.
- **Shared database, separate schema** — supported via datasource naming. One physical database, one connection pool, logical separation through schema prefixes. Middle ground between operational simplicity and isolation.
- **Shared database, row-level** — every table gets a `tenantId` column and every query gets scoped. Wheels supports it via default scopes, but this model requires the most discipline regardless of framework. The framework can't protect you from a hand-rolled join that forgets the where clause.

## Why "in the framework" matters

The resolver lives at the datasource layer, which means every other in-core feature composes with it by construction. The background job queue, association loading, the DI request-scoped service container — none of them needed extra integration work to be tenant-aware. They share the same datasource resolution.

Compare:

- **Rails:** `apartment` gem ([repo](https://github.com/influitive/apartment)) — community package with a long history of breaking against ORM internals across releases.
- **Laravel:** `stancl/tenancy` ([site](https://tenancyforlaravel.com/)) — middleware and per-request init overhead from a package.
- **Django:** `django-tenants` ([repo](https://github.com/django-tenants/django-tenants)) — schema-only by default.

Each works, none is part of the framework. Wheels 4.0 puts the resolver in core because tenant-awareness is a property of the request, not a feature you opt into.

## Tenant-aware background jobs

This is the part that separates a framework-level solution from a plugin-level one. When a job is enqueued from tenant A's request, the tenant context is persisted with the job. When the worker picks it up — different process, different host, hours later — the framework restores tenant context before `perform()` runs.

```cfm
component extends="wheels.Job" {
    function config() {
        super.config();
        this.queue = "reports";
    }
    public void function perform(struct data = {}) {
        var orders = model("Order").findAll();   // tenant A's orders, automatically
        generateMonthlyReport(orders);
    }
}
```

No "tenant ID as payload field" ceremony. No `with_tenant(tenant) { ... }` wrapper around every `perform` body. No unit test that accidentally passes because it happened to run against the right default datasource. The `model("Order").findAll()` call inside the job behaves exactly the way it would inside the controller that enqueued it.

Pairs naturally with yesterday's post on the [DB-backed job queue](https://blog.wheels.dev/posts/background-jobs-without-redis/).

## When NOT to use framework-level multi-tenancy

Honesty clause. There are places where you *want* to escape the tenant context, and pretending otherwise makes the feature worse, not better.

- **Admin and ops consoles.** The whole point of an internal admin is cross-tenant visibility. "Which tenants signed up this week?" "Which tenants are approaching their rate limit?" Those queries cannot run inside a tenant's datasource. Exit the tenant context explicitly, or wire a dedicated system datasource for admin reads.
- **Cross-tenant reports and billing.** Same rule. Monthly invoicing, aggregate usage metrics, platform-wide analytics — these live in a system-level datasource with deliberate, audited queries. Treat the escape hatch as a deliberate exception, not a framework fight.

The framework makes the right thing easy. It doesn't make the cross-cutting thing impossible. Both matter.

## Migrations and seeding per tenant

Each tenant database gets the same migration set. `wheels dbmigrate latest` targets per-tenant datasources — either one at a time or across all registered tenants in a loop. Seeding respects the active tenant context, so `seeds.cfm` runs against the right database without special casing.

Adding a tenant: create the datasource, run migrations, run seeds. Removing a tenant: destroy the datasource. There is no row-leak risk to audit because there are no rows to leave behind.

## Operational story

Per-datasource backup and restore. Per-datasource scaling. A tenant hammering CPU doesn't starve the others. A tenant requesting GDPR erasure is a `DROP DATABASE` away from complete.

One detail: the rate limiter's database storage lives on the application datasource, not per-tenant. That's deliberate — you want cross-tenant rate-limit visibility for abuse detection, and you don't want to provision that table inside every customer database.

## Links

- [Full audit § Multi-tenancy](https://github.com/wheels-dev/wheels/blob/develop/docs/releases/wheels-4.0-audit.md)
- [PR #1951 — Tenant-aware datasource switching](https://github.com/wheels-dev/wheels/pull/1951)
- [Yesterday's post — DB-backed job queue](https://blog.wheels.dev/posts/background-jobs-without-redis/)
- [Multi-tenancy guide](https://guides.wheels.dev/v4-0-0-snapshot/digging-deeper/multi-tenancy/)
- [Background jobs guide](https://guides.wheels.dev/v4-0-0-snapshot/digging-deeper/background-jobs/)
- [Middleware pipeline](https://guides.wheels.dev/v4-0-0-snapshot/core-concepts/middleware-pipeline/)

## Question for the thread

If you're running production multi-tenant SaaS today, what's your tenant identity source — subdomain, path prefix, header, JWT claim, or something else? And how does it interact with your auth layer? That's the area we expect 4.0.x to want the most polish.

**Read the full post:** https://blog.wheels.dev/posts/multi-tenancy-built-in/
